pull.title: wallet: make migration more robust against failures
pull.body:
This is just me finding a few more edge cases after #34156 and #34176

The goal of the PR is to handle failures in a controlled way. Just so the process can automatically restore the original wallet without requiring user manual intervention.

The covered cases are:

1. During `DoMigration()`: There are methods that can throw exceptions and abruptly abort the process. 
Instead of crashing (GUI) or returning a generic exception, we now will catch and return the error gracefully. This lets the process restore the original wallet automatically.

2. Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory throws a filesystem exception and skips cleanup.
 Now the process will fail gracefully with a clear error msg, and automatically restore the original wallet.

3. Any failure during `MigrateToSQLite` requires user manual intervention. 
Now the original wallet db will remain untouched, and only be updated once the sqlite db creation fully succeeds.

Code review ACK 406c14db5b16c2e1befdef76d6debd0b0ca4f6c2. I think this looks good, and all the changes here seem safe, but given complexity of the code would want to have another pass of review to have more confidence there are no bugs.

On the approach: first 4 commits look great and straightforwardly improve error handling. Initial concern i had earlier about trying to predict whether paths were writable is resolved and well handled. 

The last commit should also be a net improvement, but is more of a mixed bag. The last commit provides a potentially significant benefit because it delays deleting the original wallet database until the new sqlite database is fully created, so if there are errors creating it, the old wallet will be left in place, and it it can be migrated again later (or dumped or opened in an old version of bitcoin core) without the user manually needing to restore from the backup file.

The downside of the last commit is it adds more complexity to code that is already pretty complex, and leaves filesystem in a slightly messier state because if creating and populating the sqlite database fails there will now be two copies of the original bdb database instead of one.

More ideally the code would get rid of all these deletes and renames and backups and restores and just leave the original data exactly where it is during the migration, writing the new data to temporary directory. Then do simple renames if the migration succeeds, renaming the old wallet to have a migrated_<timestamp> suffix and renaming the new wallet directories in its place.
@furszy can you rebase and address @ryanofsky's comments?

Updated per feedback. Thanks @ryanofsky! sorry for the delay.

> More ideally the code would get rid of all these deletes and renames and backups and restores and just leave the original data exactly where it is during the migration, writing the new data to temporary directory. Then do simple renames if the migration succeeds, renaming the old wallet to have a migrated_ suffix and renaming the new wallet directories in its place.

I had a branch for this ~2.5 years ago (it should still be in my repo fork), creating a new wallet and importing descriptors, txs, metadata there, etc. which was letting us remove `MigrateToSQLite` entirely, but I wasn't convinced it was ever going to be merged due to all the bugs we were continually finding within the process back then, and some other refactoring that was needed. We are much better now to retry to implement it but I hardly see such a big change landing at this point in time.

Code review 3ca388f099c6a161faa40bf8b91c5aa89cb5b11d. Thanks for the updates! This is very close and a clear improvement over master in most failure cases: writing all records before removing the original file, and rolling back on exceptions, both look good.

I'd like to see [the stale journal issue](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4484088024) fixed before ACKing, since it is the one case where copying the new database into place can corrupt a wallet that master would migrate correctly. The fix should be small. [The copy_file failure case](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4481335673) and the commit message suggestions would also be good to address, but I wouldn't block on them.

This is possibly orthogonal, but I just had the thought that maybe we can achieve some additional robustness in migration by first migrating to an in-memory sqlite database, and then only writing that out to disk when migration is successful. Then we may be able to sidestep the whole issue of needing to automatically restore the original legacy wallet file by not removing it until we are sure the new database is good.

Still, I think this PR contains some good changes that worth to get merged even if we move towards that direction.

Code review ACK 8a9c3af0eb7df50f38ca511491d3d0d1e47f7fb7. This is a clear improvement over master, which deletes the original database before writing the new one. Now a directory wallet stays untouched until a single rename replaces it, exceptions roll back to the backup, and the stale journal case is handled.

Thanks for the quick and thorough update! None of the inline comments need to block this, but the ones I think matter most are:

- [The `return false` vs. throw contract](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4551983828): a false return from `MigrateToSQLite` skips the restore, so any failure after the original is replaced has to throw. Nothing enforces that, and it would be easy for a future change to get wrong ([example](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4553133860)).
- [Failures that still need a manual restore](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4551983828): a plain-file wallet whose original is erased before the move, and the reopen `Assert`.
- Unexpected states that are silently ignored, like [cleanup failures](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4553153518) and [a temporary directory left behind after a successful move](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4553133860).

The [Ralph review](https://review.fish.foo/traces/34193-8a9c3af0eb7df50f38ca511491d3d0d1e47f7fb7-2505-5.html) was also helpful here and caught a few of the smaller issues noted inline.

author furszy <matiasfurszyfer@protonmail.com> 1788378081 -0400
committer furszy <matiasfurszyfer@protonmail.com> 1794601459 -0500

wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures

Currently, MigrateToSQLite loads all BDB records into memory,
then deletes the original database just to create the sqlite
db in the same place, and finally writes all cached records
to it.

This is not really the best because it removes the original db
before making sure the sqlite one is fully built. If creation
fails, the wallet ends up partly in sqlite format with legacy
records, and the user has to restore from a backup manually.

This fixes all that by creating the sqlite db in a temporary
directory first. Then, the original BDB files are removed only
once the sqlite db is fully constructed, and the new db is
moved into the original location.

The result is that no user manual intervention is needed if
MigrateToSQLite fails as the original db stays untouched.

In commit "wallet: fail migration gracefully on non-writable wallets" (eb5e076b189aa5dadb9572f3ce7b33eb609d7b69)

Was skimming this PR and the first few commits seem reasonable, but I’d advise against the approach in the last two commits of checking whether paths are writable before writing, rather than handling write failures directly. A few concerns:

1. It masks other problems. Write failures should surface through the normal error-reporting paths with clear messages, regardless of where they originate. Pre-checks bypass those paths and can obscure or regress error reporting, especially if lower-level errors improve over time.

2. It adds unnecessary complexity. The write still has to be attempted, so the pre-check duplicates logic without simplifying the code.

3. It introduces TOCTOU risks. A path that is writable at check time may not be writable at write time.

In general, attempting the write and handling failures directly is simpler, more robust, and leads to better error reporting.

The issue here is that we are doing low-level operations. Basically, we are:
1) Loading all BDB records into memory.
2) Deleting the BDB file.
3) Creating a new sqlite db.
4) Writing all records to the new db.

The added checks are meant to avoid failing with a generic filesystem exception at step (2), during the BDB deletion, which can be located in a different directory than the sqlite one we are about to create

But.. thinking further, we could handle this differently by catching the exception directly from the `fs::remove` call instead. Let me see why I didn't do it in that way before, there must be a reason.

Also, the last commit is about not removing the original wallet until we are sure the sqlite one has at least been created successfully. If we are not able to write to disk at that point, the migration will fail anyway. This function is just the early "move everything from BDB to sqlite" step; we still need to create and store the descriptors, remove the old records, and so on.

In commit "wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures" (b9486540d774f2e07ecce93af0637d6e685a93e0)

Would it work to create the temporary database next to the original file, in `origin_db_path.parent_path()`, instead of in the wallets directory? Then it is always on the same filesystem as the destination, and the `copy_file` call below could be a `fs::rename`:

- The move becomes atomic, so a failure can't leave a partially copied `wallet.dat` behind.
- There is no need to copy a possibly large file, or for the new `copy_file` overload in `fs.h`.

In commit "wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures" (da055ca4bc59df70d034e7f528165f4d13ed06bf)

Following up on https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4481335673: with the rename, a failure here now leaves directory wallets untouched, which covers the common case. From reading the code, two narrower cases still need a manual restore from the `.legacy.bak` file:

- For a plain-file wallet, the original is erased first, so if `MoveDatabase` then fails, `fail()` also deletes the new database and `MigrateLegacyToDescriptor` returns the error without restoring the backup.
- If the rename succeeds but reopening fails, the `Assert` in `MoveDatabase` crashes the node. The close and reopen also open a new window: migration doesn't reserve the wallet name the way loading does, so a concurrent `loadwallet` for the same wallet could take the database's exclusive lock in between. The [Ralph review](https://review.fish.foo/traces/34193-8a9c3af0eb7df50f38ca511491d3d0d1e47f7fb7-2505-5.html#:~:text=Post%2Dinstall%20database%20reopen%20failures%20abort%20the%20node) reports this case too and pointed out the `loadwallet` race.

Neither is a regression, so I don't think they need to block this, but it would be nice if failures after the original is erased or replaced went through the restore path added in "wallet: migration, restore backup if an exception is thrown", for example by returning an error from `MoveDatabase` instead of asserting and throwing from `MigrateToSQLite` in these cases.

More generally, `MigrateLegacyToDescriptor` treats a false return from `MigrateToSQLite` as "the original is untouched" and skips the restore, while an exception gets the full rollback. That makes it easy for a future change to add a `return false` after the point of no return without noticing ([the comment on the final cleanup](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4553133860) is one place where this matters). It would be less fragile if the caller decided based on whether the original was replaced, for example with an output parameter set right after the move, instead of on how the failure was reported, or at least if `MigrateToSQLite` documented that it may only return false while the original is untouched.

In commit "wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures" (da055ca4bc59df70d034e7f528165f4d13ed06bf)

The commit message still describes an earlier version of this change: it doesn't say the temporary directory is now next to the original database (which is what makes the rename possible), it says the original files are removed before the new database is moved in, when for directory wallets the rename now replaces the original directly, and it doesn't mention the leftover journal cleanup. Maybe something like:

```
Currently, MigrateToSQLite loads all BDB records into memory, deletes the original database, creates the sqlite database in its place and writes the records to it. If anything fails after the delete, the wallet is left partly in sqlite format with legacy records, and the user has to restore the backup manually.

Instead, build the sqlite database in a temporary directory next to the original database file, and once all records are written, rename it into place. For wallet directories the rename replaces the original wallet.dat atomically, so a failure at any earlier point leaves the original untouched. A wallet that is a plain file becomes a wallet directory, which cannot replace the file atomically, so the original file is erased just before the move.

Before the move, remove any leftover journal at the destination, since SQLite would roll it back into the new database when it is opened and corrupt it.
```
